* **`List()`** – used for discrete (enumerated) knob values.  
* **`Range()`** – used for continuous (numeric) knob values.

API: Multi-Config Specification
===============

The core value of RapidFire AI is in the ability to launch, compare, and dynamically 
control multiple configurations (configs) in one go. 
It is already common practice in AI to do hyperparameter sweeps via grid search, 
random search, or AutoML heuristics to generate knob values. 

RapidFire AI generalizes that notion to any type of config knobs, not just  
regular hyperparameters, but also base model architectures, prompt schemes, 
LoRA adapters, and optimizers (for training), as well as data chunking, embedding, 
retrieval, reranking, generation, and prompt schemes (for RAG) and any other 
user-defined knobs. 


Knob Set Generators
-------

To create a multi-config specification, you need two things: **knob set generators** for 
knob values and **config group generators** that take a config with set-valued knobs 
to generate groups of full configs.
Note that the return types of the knob set generators are internal to RapidFire AI and 
they are usable only within the context of the config group generators below.



Config Group Generators
-----

We currently support two common config group generators: :func:`RFGridSearch()` for grid search 
and :func:`RFRandomSearch()` for random search. 

More support for AutoML heuristics such as SHA, HyperOpt, as well as an integration with 
the popular AutoML library Optuna are coming soon. 
Likewise for RAG/context engineering, we also plan to support the AutoML heuristic syftr.


.. py:function:: RFGridSearch(configs: Dict[str, Any] | List[Dict[str, Any]], trainer_type: str = "SFT" | "DPO" | "GRPO" | None)

	:param configs: A config dictionary with :func:`List()` for at least one knob; can be a list of such config dictionaries too.
	:type configs: Dict[str, Any] | List[Dict[str, Any]]
Again, the only difference here is that the individual arguments (knobs) can be :class:`List` 
valued or :class:`Range` valued in :class:`RFGROConfig`. 
That is how you can specify a base set of knob combinations from which a config group can 
be produced. Also read :doc:`the Multi-Config Specification page</configs>`.
Other than the multi-config specification, this class preserves all semantics of 
Hugging Face's GRPO trainer under the hood. 

**Example:**

.. code-block:: python

	# Based on the GRPO tutorial notebook
	RFGRPOConfig(
		learning_rate=5e-6,
		warmup_ratio=0.1,
		weight_decay=0.1,
		max_grad_norm=0.1,
		adam_beta1=0.9,
		adam_beta2=0.99,
		lr_scheduler_type = "linear",
		per_device_train_batch_size=4,
		gradient_accumulation_steps=4,
		num_generations=8,
		optim ="adamw_8bit",
		num_train_epochs=2,
		max_prompt_length=1024,
		max_completion_length=1024,
		logging_steps=2,
		eval_steps=5,
	)
API: Generator Configs
===============

RapidFire AI supports both self-hosted open LLMs and closed model LLM APIs as the generator. 
As of this writing, it wraps around the model config of vLLM for the former and the OpenAI API for the latter. 
We plan to expand support for more generator plugins, including Gemini and Claude APIs, based on feedback. 


RFvLLMModelConfig
------

This is a wrapper around vLLM's :class:`config` and :class:`SamplingParams` classes. 
The full list of their arguments are available on `this page <https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/api/vllm/config/index.html>`__ 
and `this page <https://docs.vllm.ai/en/v0.6.4/dev/sampling_params.html>`__, respectively.
API: Trainer Configs
===============

RapidFire AI's core APIs for trainer specifications are all thin wrappers around the 
corresponding APIs of Hugging Face's `TRL <https://huggingface.co/docs/trl/index>`__ libraries.

Finally, apart from the Generator, the following knobs can also be included in your eval config dictionary. Each of

API: Prompt Manager and Other Eval Config Knobs
===============

------

This class wraps around some LangChain APIs to manage dynamic few-shot example selection. It provides semantic

RapidFire AI’s **adaptive execution engine** turns the ordinary “run‑one‑config‑to‑completion‑then‑run‑the‑next” workflow on its head.  

### What traditional sequential execution does  
* **One‑config‑at‑a‑time** – For SFT/RFT or for RAG evals the system waits until a configuration has processed the **entire dataset for every epoch** (or the whole eval set) before starting the next configuration.  
* **No early insight** – Because the full dataset must finish, you only see the final metrics after the run is done, which can waste GPU time or token spend on poorly‑performing configs.  
* **Coarse‑grained scheduling** – Generic MLOps tools treat each run as a monolithic job and place it on a GPU/CPU without any ability to pause, swap, or re‑allocate resources while it is in flight.

### What RapidFire AI’s adaptive engine does instead  

| Aspect | Adaptive execution engine (RapidFire AI) | Traditional sequential execution |
|--------|-------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------|
| **Data handling** | Randomly **shards** the training/evaluation set into “chunks” (e.g., 4 shards). Each config works on **one shard at a time** and the scheduler **cycles through all shards** across configs. | Processes the **whole dataset** for a config before moving on. |
| **Parallelism** | Multiple configs run **concurrently** on different shards, with the engine automatically swapping adapters, base models, and memory between GPUs/DRAM (the thin gray‑box swap overhead is **< 5 %** of total runtime). | Configs run **sequentially**, even on a single GPU; any parallelism is limited to low‑level data or model parallelism, not across configs. |
| **Real‑time feedback** | As shards are processed, **online aggregation** produces **estimated metrics and confidence intervals** in real time, letting you see early performance trends. | You must wait for the **full run** to finish before any metric is available. |
| **Interruptible / interactive control (IC Ops)** | You can **stop** a non‑promising run, put it on a wait queue, **resume** it later, **clone** a high‑performing run, **modify** knobs, and **warm‑start** the clone with the parent’s parameters—all while the system is still running other shards. | No built‑in way to pause, clone, or adjust a job that is already executing; you would have to kill the run and start a new one. |
| **Scheduler intelligence** | The engine **automatically assigns shards to GPUs/CPUs**, manages memory caching and spill‑to‑disk, and balances multi‑GPU usage without user intervention. | Users must manually manage data‑parallel (DDP/FSDP) or task‑parallel (W&B, Ray Tune) setups; GPUs can sit idle if the workload is not well‑balanced. |
| **Overhead** | Swapping overhead is minimal – measured at **less than 5 %** of total runtime thanks to efficient shared‑memory caching. | No swapping, but the sequential nature means you waste the full cost of a whole epoch before you can decide whether to continue. |

### Summarized difference  
RapidFire AI’s adaptive engine **shards** the data and interleaves the execution of many configurations, giving you **early, statistically‑sound evaluation results** and **dynamic, interruptible control** over runs. Traditional sequential execution processes each configuration **end‑to‑end** before any other starts, offering no early visibility, no real‑time control, and often poorer resource utilisation. This makes RapidFire AI dramatically faster and more cost‑effective for multi‑config experiments.

What Makes RapidFire AI Different?
==============

The crux of RapidFire AI's difference is in its *adaptive execution engine*: it enables "interruptible"
execution of configurations across GPUs/CPUs. To do so, it first shards the training and/or evaluation 
dataset randomly into "chunks" (also called "shards").
Then instead of waiting for a run to see the whole dataset for all epochs (for SFT/RFT) or for full 
eval metrics calculation (for RAG evals), RapidFire AI schedules all runs on *one shard at a time*, 
and then cycles through all shards.
The Power of Dynamic Real-Time Control
------------

Our adaptive execution engine also enables a powerful new capability: *dynamic real-time 
control over runs in flight*. We call this Interactive Control Operations, or IC Ops for short. 

*Stop* non-promising runs at any point--they will be put on a wait queue. *Resume* any later if 
you want to revisit it. *Clone* high-performing runs from the dashboard and *Modify* the 
configuration knobs as you see fit to try new variations. *Warm start* the clone's parameters 
with the parent's to give them a headstart in learning behavior. 
Under the hood, RapidFire AI automatically manages how runs and chunks are placed on GPUs, 
freeing you to focus fully on the logic of your AI experiment rather than wrestling with 
low-level systems issue to parallelize your work.
.. image:: /images/gantt-1gpu.png
   :width: 800px

In the above figure, all 3 model configs are shown for 1 epoch. RapidFire AI is set to use 4 chunks.
So, before model config 3 (M3) even starts in the sequential approach, RapidFire AI already shows you 
the learning behaviors of all 3 configs on the first 2-3 chunks. 
The overhead of swapping, represented by the thin gray box, is minimal, less than 5% of the runtime,
as per our measurements--thanks to our new efficient memory management techniques.

For inference evals for RAG/context engineering, such sharded execution means RapidFire AI surfaces eval metrics 
sooner based on a statistical technique known as *online aggregation* from the database systems literature.
Basically, see estimated values and confidence intervals for all eval metrics in real time as the shards 
get processed, ultimately converging to the exact metrics on the full dataset.


The Power of Dynamic Real-Time Control
------------
Check out :doc:`the step-by-step walkthrough page</walkthrough>` and watch the usage video for details.



To learn more about the *adaptive execution engine* that differentiates RapidFire AI, powers its hyperparallelized 
execution, and enable IC Ops on running configs, :doc:`check out this page</difference>`.

Takeaways
----------

RapidFire AI transforms RAG/context engineering evals from a slow, tedious 
guessing game into a fast, dynamic engineering process. 
With real-time metrics, statistically sound confidence intervals, and dynamic control, 
you can compare far more configs efficiently, make data-driven decisions, and 
optimize across the Pareto frontier of eval metrics, cost, and time.
Suppose you have only 1 GPU, say an A100 or H100, and you want to run SFT on a Llama model. 
Current tools force you to run one config after another *sequentially* as shown in the (simplified) illustration below. 
In contrast, by operating on shards, RapidFire AI offers a far more concurrent learning experience by 
automatically *swapping* adapters (and base models, if needed) across GPU(s) and DRAM. 
It does this via efficient shared memory-based caching mechanisms that can spill to disk when needed.

.. image:: /images/gantt-1gpu.png
   :width: 800px
* Even for a prior deployed model, one may need to adapt knobs over time as the data distribution evolves (e.g., concept drift), application schema evolves (e.g., data collection process changes), newer/better models emerge (e.g., smaller but more capable LLMs), etc.


Generic MLOps tools treat a run as a generic monolithic job and schedule them at a coarse granularity, 
leading to a disconnect between what is needed for customization and the execution layer.
IC Ops alter this status quo by giving you a whole new level of control over runs in flight. 

No need to juggle disparate tools for data-parallelism (DDP), model-parallelism (FSDP / DeepSpeed), or 
task-parallelism (W&B, Ray Tune, etc.).
RapidFire AI's execution engine handles lower level scheduling and orchestration of run adaptively 
to enable IC Ops.



Semantics of IC Ops
-----
Overview of RapidFire AI Package
==============

RapidFire AI is a new AI experiment execution framework that transforms your LLM pipeline customization 
from slow, sequential processes into rapid, intelligent workflows with hyperparallelized execution, 
dynamic real-time experiment control, and automatic backend optimization.

For *RAG and context engineering evals*, start here: :doc:`Install and Get Started: RAG and Context Engineering</walkthroughrag>`.

For *SFT and RFT/post-training workflows*, start here: :doc:`Install and Get Started: SFT/RFT</walkthroughft>`.


RapidFire AI is the first system of its kind to establish live three-way communication between the IDE
where the experiment is launched, a metrics display/control dashboard, and a multi-core/multi-GPU execution backend.

.. image:: /images/rf-usage.png
   :width: 800px
Online Aggregation for Evals
============================

When evaluating RAG/context eng. pipelines, traditional batch evals processing forces you to 
wait for the whole dataset to be processed by a config before seeing its results. 
For expensive LLM-based generators (both closed model APIs and self-hosted models) that can lead
to wastage of a lot of token spend and/or a lot of GPU resources before you realize that a config 
yields poor eval metrics. 
That can inhibit experimentation on config knobs due to the time and/or costs involved, 
ultimately hurting eval metrics and stalling AI applications.

RapidFire AI transforms the status quo by adapting the powerful idea of **online aggregation** 
from database systems research to LLM evals. 
Our adaptive execution engine, :doc:`as described on this page</difference>`, automatically 
shards the data and processes multiple configs in parallel, one shard at a time, with 
efficient swapping techniques.
RapidFire AI supports multi-GPU setups natively. Here is a (simplified) illustration of 
sequential execution with Data Parallelism (say, with DDP or FSDP) vs. Task Parallelism 
(say, with Weights & Biases) vs. RapidFire AI, both without and with IC Ops. 
Our scheduler navigates multiple GPUs automatically so that you need not worry if any GPU 
is underutilized, e.g., like in the case of Task Parallelism for the workload shown below.

.. image:: /images/gantt-2gpu.png
   :width: 800px

Likewise, for RAG/context engineering evals on self-hosted LLMs, the above multi-GPU 
scheduling optimizations also apply out of the box, albeit analogous to a single epoch. 
When using only closed model APIs such as OpenAI, RapidFire AI's scheduler automatically 
optimizes how CPU cores and the token rate limits are apportioned across configs. 
This will help avoid wastage of token spend on unproductive RAG configs and help you 
redirect the spend to more productive RAG configs in real time.

**RFGridSearch vs. RFRandomSearch – how they treat knob values**

| Aspect | **RFGridSearch** | **RFRandomSearch** |
|--------|------------------|--------------------|
| **Allowed knob types** | Each knob may be a **single value** *or* a **`List()`** of discrete values. **`Range()`** values are **not allowed** – using a range will raise an error. | Each knob may be a **single value**, a **`List()`** of discrete values **or** a **`Range()`** of continuous values. |
| **How combinations are built** | The generator creates a **grid**: it exhaustively combines every value from each `List()` (or the single value) to produce all possible configurations. | The generator performs **IID random sampling**: for each run it independently picks one value from each knob’s discrete set (if a `List()`) **or** samples uniformly from the continuous interval (if a `Range()`). This process is repeated `num_runs` times to produce distinct random combos. |
| **Sampling semantics** | Deterministic – the full Cartesian product of the listed values. | Stochastic – uniform random draw from each knob’s domain (discrete or continuous), repeated independently for each run. |

**Citation from the context**

- For **RFGridSearch**: “For :func:`RFGridSearch()`, each knob can have either a single value or a :func:`List()` of values but **no knob should have :func:`Range()` of values**; otherwise, it will error out.”  
- For **RFRandomSearch**: “For :func:`RFRandomSearch()`, each knob can have either a single value, or a :func:`List()` of values, **or a :func:`Range()` of values**. The semantics of sampling are independently‑identically‑distributed (IID)… we uniformly randomly pick a value from each discrete set and from each continuous set to construct the knob combination for one run. Then we repeat that sampling process in an IID way to accumulate `num_runs` distinct combinations.”

Thus, the key difference is that **RFGridSearch only works with fixed lists (no ranges) and enumerates every possible combination**, whereas **RFRandomSearch can also accept ranges and builds configurations by randomly sampling each knob’s value for each run**.

.. py:function:: RFGridSearch(configs: Dict[str, Any] | List[Dict[str, Any]], trainer_type: str = "SFT" | "DPO" | "GRPO" | None)

	:param configs: A config dictionary with :func:`List()` for at least one knob; can be a list of such config dictionaries too.
	:type configs: Dict[str, Any] | List[Dict[str, Any]]
Again, the only difference here is that the individual arguments (knobs) can be :class:`List` 
valued or :class:`Range` valued in :class:`RFGROConfig`. 
That is how you can specify a base set of knob combinations from which a config group can 
be produced. Also read :doc:`the Multi-Config Specification page</configs>`.
Other than the multi-config specification, this class preserves all semantics of 
Hugging Face's GRPO trainer under the hood. 

**Example:**

.. code-block:: python

	# Based on the GRPO tutorial notebook
	RFGRPOConfig(
		learning_rate=5e-6,
		warmup_ratio=0.1,
		weight_decay=0.1,
		max_grad_norm=0.1,
		adam_beta1=0.9,
		adam_beta2=0.99,
		lr_scheduler_type = "linear",
		per_device_train_batch_size=4,
		gradient_accumulation_steps=4,
		num_generations=8,
		optim ="adamw_8bit",
		num_train_epochs=2,
		max_prompt_length=1024,
		max_completion_length=1024,
		logging_steps=2,
		eval_steps=5,
	)
The difference here is that the individual arguments (knobs) can be :class:`List` valued or 
:class:`Range` valued in an :class:`RFvLLMModelConfig`. 
That is how you can specify a base set of knob combinations from which a config group can 
be produced. Also read :doc:`the Multi-Config Specification page</configs>`.

.. py:class:: RFvLLMModelConfig
:param seed: Seed for random sampling of knob values to construct combinations. Default is 42.
	:type seed: int, optional 


**Notes:**

For :func:`RFGridSearch()`, each knob can have either a single value or a :func:`List()` of values but no knob 
should have :func:`Range()` of values; otherwise, it will error out.

For :func:`RFRandomSearch()`, each knob can have either a single value, or a :func:`List()` of values, or a 
 :func:`Range()` of values. The semantics of sampling are independently-identically-distributed (IID), i.e.,
we uniformly randomly pick a value from each discrete set and from each continuous set to construct the 
knob combination for one run. 
Then we repeat that sampling process in an IID way to accumulate :code:`num_runs` distinct combinations.

Note that the return types of the config group generators are internal to RapidFire AI and they are usable only 
within the context of :func:`run_fit()` or :func:`run_evals()` in the :class:`Experiment` class.
Edit any knobs, e.g., learning rate, LoRA rank, or even base model as if you are injecting 
that new run config from code, except this is done conveniently from the metrics dashboard itself. 
As of this writing, we only support providing a single config for this IC Op.
Soon we will support providing a config-group generator such as :code:`RFGridSearch()` or
:code:`RFRandomSearch()` as well in the IC Op panel itself akin to the launching code.

You can also **warm-start** a clone using its parent's weights if you'd like. 
Warm-started clones inherit their parent's learning behavior so far and thus, they can reach better 
eval metrics faster. 
Note that warm starting is only allowed if the clones have *identical* neural architecture as the 
parent, including LoRA adapters; otherwise, it will error out.

When you are ready with your clone's config, click "Submit" to execute this IC Op.

	# Based on GSM8K chatbot tutorial notebook; specify your INSTRUCTIONS beforehand

===============

RFPromptManager
------

This class wraps around some LangChain APIs to manage dynamic few-shot example selection. It provides semantic 
similarity-based example selection to construct prompts with the most relevant examples for each input query.

The individual arguments (knobs) can be :class:`List` valued or :class:`Range` valued in an :class:`RFPromptManager`. 
That is how you can specify a base set of knob combinations from which a config group can be produced.

.. py:class:: RFPromptManager

  :param instructions: The main instructions for the prompt that guide the generator's behavior. This sets the overall task description and role for the assistant. Either this or :code:`instructions_file_path` must be provided.
  :type instructions: str, optional
The difference here is that the individual arguments (knobs) can be :class:`List` valued or 
:class:`Range` valued in an :class:`RFOpenAIAPIModelConfig`.

be produced. Also read :doc:`the Multi-Config Specification page</configs>`.

Note that one :class:`RFLangChainRagSpec` object can have at most one :code:`document_loader` to specify the base data.

* If :code:`retriever` is provided, it is used as is. No need for :code:`document_loader`, :code:`text_splitter`, or :code:`vector_store_cfg`.
We currently support two common knob set generators: :func:`List()` for a discrete 
set of values and :func:`Range()` for sampling from a continuous value interval.


.. py:function:: List(values: List[Any])

	:param values: List of discrete values for a knob; all values must be the same python data type.

.. py:function:: Range(start: int | float, end: int | float, dtype: str = "int" | "float")

**Setting up RapidFire AI for RAG‑evaluation on a CPU‑only machine**  

You can run the full RapidFire AI RAG workflow without any GPU hardware as long as you use **only closed‑model APIs (e.g., OpenAI)** for embedding and generation. The steps are the same as a “full installation”, except you skip any GPU‑related concerns. Below is the exact procedure taken from the documentation, with the relevant excerpts quoted.

---

### 1. Prepare a Python 3.12+ environment  

```bash
python3 --version   # must show 3.12.x   (see “Requires Python 3.12+”)
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
```

> *“Requires Python 3.12+. Ensure that `python3` resolves to Python 3.12 before creating the venv.”* (Overview of RapidFire AI Package)

---

### 2. Install the RapidFire AI OSS package  

```bash
pip install rapidfireai
```

> *“Obtain the RapidFire AI OSS package from pypi (includes all dependencies) and ensure it is installed correctly.”*

After installation, verify the version:

```bash
rapidfireai --version
# Expected output: RapidFire AI 0..14.0
```

> *“Verify it prints the following: RapidFire AI 0..14.0”* (Installation section)

*Optional clean‑up*: The current Hugging‑Face XET issue requires uninstalling that extra:

```bash
pip uninstall -y hf-xet
```

> *“Due to current issue: https://github.com/huggingface/xet-core/issues/527”* (Installation section)

---

### 3. Initialise RapidFire AI for RAG‑specific dependencies  

Run the init command **once per virtual environment** (or when you change GPUs – not needed here).

```bash
rapidfireai init --evals
```

> *“Run the following commands to initialize rapidfireai to use the correct dependencies for RAG evals:”* (Full Installation → Step 1)

---

### 4. Provide your OpenAI API key  

Since you are not using self‑hosted models, you must supply a valid OpenAI key in the config you will pass to the notebooks / scripts. The docs note:

> *“If you plan to use only OpenAI APIs … you must provide a valid OpenAI API key via a config argument as shown in the GSM8K and SciFact tutorial notebooks.”* (Full Installation intro)

Insert the key in the notebook’s `config` object or export it as an environment variable (`OPENAI_API_KEY`), following the tutorial examples.

---

### 5. Start the RapidFire AI services (frontend + API server)  

```bash
rapidfireai start
```

You should see a log of ~50 lines that includes:

```
RapidFire Frontend is ready
Open your browser and navigate to: http://0.0.0.0:8853
Press Ctrl+C to stop all services
```

> *“It should print about 50 lines, including the following… RapidFire Frontend is ready… Open your browser and navigate to: http://0.0.0.0:8853”* (Full Installation → Step 1)

The dashboard is accessible in a local browser even though the backend is CPU‑only.

---

### 6. Run your RAG evaluation notebooks or scripts  

Now you can import the package in any notebook/script, define your RAG configs, and launch them. The **online aggregation** engine works without GPUs; it will automatically schedule work across CPU cores and respect OpenAI token‑rate limits.

> *“When using only closed model APIs such as OpenAI, RapidFire AI's scheduler automatically optimizes how CPU cores and the token rate limits are apportioned across configs.”* (Full Installation → Multi‑GPU note)

---

### 7. (Optional) Gracefully stop the server when finished  

```bash
rapidfireai stop
```

> *“If you kill the rapidfireai server forcibly without graceful stopping … you might lose some experiment artifacts.”* (Takeaways)

---

## TL;DR Checklist for a GPU‑less setup

| Action | Command | Why it matters |
|--------|---------|----------------|
| Verify Python 3.12 | `python3 --version` | Required runtime |
| Create & activate venv | `python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate` | Isolate dependencies |
| Install RapidFire AI | `pip install rapidfireai` | Gets the package & deps |
| Init eval dependencies | `rapidfireai init --evals` | Sets up RAG‑specific libs |
| Supply OpenAI key | export `OPENAI_API_KEY=…` or config arg | Needed for generation/embedding |
| Start services | `rapidfireai start` | Launches API + dashboard |
| Run notebooks / scripts | (use `rapidfireai` API) | Perform RAG evaluation |
| Stop services | `rapidfireai stop` | Clean shutdown |

Following these steps gives you a fully functional RapidFire AI RAG evaluation environment on a machine **without any GPUs**. The system will run on CPUs, automatically manage token‑rate limits for OpenAI, and provide the same real‑time metrics dashboards described in the docs.

RapidFire AI’s Interactive Control (IC) Ops provide four distinct actions you can take on runs that are already executing:

1. **Stop** – pause a non‑promising run and place it on a wait queue.  
2. **Resume** – later restart a run that was previously stopped.  
3. **Clone‑Modify** – duplicate (“clone”) a high‑performing run, optionally changing its configuration knobs (the “modify” step) and warm‑starting it from the parent’s parameters.  
4. **Delete** – permanently remove a run.

These are the four IC Operations explicitly listed in the documentation:

> “We currently support 4 IC Ops: Stop, Resume, Clone‑Modify, and Delete.”【source】

The **`preprocess_fn`** is the user‑supplied routine that “prepares the inputs to be given to the generator model.” It is called **once per batch, before any text is generated**, so that you can reshape, tokenize, or otherwise ready the data that will be fed to the LLM.

When the system calls this function it automatically **injects three arguments**:

| Argument | Type (as shown in the signature) | What it contains |
|----------|----------------------------------|-------------------|
| `batch` | `dict[str, list]` | A dictionary holding the current batch of examples (field names → lists of values). |
| `rag` | `RFLangChainRagSpec` | The RAG (retrieval‑augmented generation) specification for the leaf config being evaluated. |
| `prompt_manager` | `RFPromptManager` | The prompt manager associated with that leaf config. |

The full signature given in the docs is:

```python
def preprocess_fn(batch: dict[str, list],
                  rag: RFLangChainRagSpec,
                  prompt_manager: RFPromptManager) -> dict[str, list]:
    ...
```

Thus, **`preprocess_fn`** transforms the raw batch (using the supplied RAG spec and prompt manager if needed) into the final format that the generator model will consume during the `run_evals` pipeline.

API: User-Provided Functions for Run Evals
===============

Users can provide the following custom functions as part of their eval config to be used in :func:`run_evals()`.
Note that each leaf config can have its own set of functions for all of these.


Preprocess Function
-------------------

Mandatory user-provided function to prepare the inputs to be given to the generator model. 
It is invoked for each batch during the evaluation process before generation.
Pass it directly to the :code:`preprocess_fn` key in your eval config dictionary.

The system injects into this function the batch data, as well as the RAG spec and 
the prompt manager of an individual leaf config.


.. py:function:: preprocess_fn(batch: dict[str, list], rag: RFLangChainRagSpec, prompt_manager: RFPromptManager) -> dict[str, list]

   :param batch: Dictionary with a batch of examples with dataset field names as keys and lists as values
   :type batch: dict[str, list]
For more details on the four user-given functions listed below, see :doc:`the API: User-Provided Functions for Run Evals page</evalsfunctions>`.

For more details on the semantics of the online aggregation strategy arguments listed below, see :doc:`the Online Aggregation for Evals page</onlineagg>`.


**batch_size** : int
	Number of examples to process in one batch for GPU efficiency (if applicable)

**preprocess_fn** : Callable
	User-given function to preprocess a batch of examples; an eval config's RagSpec and PromptManager are input by the system

**postprocess_fn** : Callable, optional
	User-given function to postprocess a batch of examples and generations; a single cfg is passed as input by the system

**compute_metrics_fn** : Callable
	User-given evaluation function to compute eval metrics per batch
def sample_postprocess_fn(batch: dict[str, list]) -> dict[str, list]:
		"""Function to postprocess outputs produced by generator model"""

		batch["ground_truth_documents"] = [
			qrels[qrels["query_id"] == query_id]["corpus_id"].tolist()
			for query_id in batch["query_id"]
		]
		batch["answer"] = [extract_solution(answer) for answer in batch["generated_text"]]
		return batch



Eval Compute Metrics Function
-------------------------

Mandatory user-provided function to compute eval metrics on a given batch of (postprocessed) examples, 
which is injected by the system. 
It should return metrics computed over the batch as a whole. 

It is invoked for each batch during the evaluation process after generation and postprocessing (if applicable). 
Pass it directly to the :code:`compute_metrics_fn` key in your eval config dictionary.


.. py:function:: eval.compute_metrics_fn(batch: dict[str, list]) -> dict[str, dict[str, Any]]
Within an experiment, you can rerun :func:`run_evals()` as many times as you want. All of them 
will be overlaid on the same plots on the ML metrics dashboard.

The :code:`config_group` argument allows you to construct various knob combinations for inference pipelines 
and launch them in one go. These pipelines can involve LLMs running on your GPUs, or OpenAI API calls, or both. 

Just like with :func:`run_fit()` above, you can provide a single config dictionary, a :code:`list` of config 
dictionaries, a config group generator output (:func:`RFGridSearch()` or :func:`RFRandomSearch()` for now), 
or even a :code:`list` with mix of configs or config group generator outputs as its elements.
Please see the :doc:`the Multi-Config Specification page</search>` for more details.
**compute_metrics_fn** : Callable
	User-given evaluation function to compute eval metrics per batch

**accumulate_metrics_fn** : Callable, optional
	User-given evaluation function to aggregate algebraic eval metrics across batches. If this is not given, all metrics provided in :code:`eval_compute_metrics_fn` will be assumed to be distributive by default.

**online_strategy_kwargs** : dict[str, Any], optional
	Parameters for evals online aggregation strategy. The dictionary must include the following keys:
	
	* :code:`"strategy_name"` (str) - Must be :code:`"normal"`, :code:`"wilson"`, or :code:`"hoeffding"`.
	* :code:`"confidence_level"` (float) - Confidence level for confidence intervals on metrics. Must be in [0,1]. Default is 0.95 (95%).
	* :code:`"use_fpc"` (bool) - Whether to apply finite population correction. Default is :code:`True`.
Postprocess Function
--------------------

Optional user-provided function to postprocess a batch of examples and their respective generated outputs, 
which is injected into this function by the system. 
This is useful for, say, extracting structured information from generations, adding ground truth data, 
or performing any transformations needed before computing metrics.

It is invoked for each batch during the evaluation process after generation and before metric computation.
Pass it directly to the :code:`postprocess_fn` key in your eval config dictionary.


.. py:function:: postprocess_fn(batch: dict[str, list]) -> dict[str, list]

   :param batch: Dictionary containing a batch of examples, including their respective generated outputs under the reserved key :code:`"generated_text"`.
   :type batch: dict[str, list]

   :return: Dictionary containing the postprocessed batch with any new or modified keys
   :rtype: dict[str, list]


**Examples:**

.. code-block:: python
Eval Accumulate Metrics Function
----------------------------

Optional user-provided function to aggregate algebraic eval metrics across all batches of the data. 
If this function is not provided, all metrics returned by :func:`eval.compute_metrics_fn()` 
will be assumed to be distributive (i.e., summed across batches) by default. Use this function 
when metrics require (weighted) averaging or other custom dataset-wide aggregation logic.

It is invoked once at the very end of the evaluation process after all batches have been processed.
Pass it directly to the :code:`accumulate_metrics_fn` key in your eval config dictionary.


.. py:function:: eval.accumulate_metrics_fn(aggregated_metrics: dict[str, list[dict[str, Any]]]) -> dict[str, dict[str, Any]]

	:type param_config: Train config-group or list as described in :doc:`the Multi-Config Specification page</configs>`

	:type num_actors: int, optional

	:param seed: Seed to control randomness for online aggregation (default: 42)
	:type seed: int, optional
Each individual config is passed as input to your :func:`create_model_fn()`. Inside it you can use whatever 
knob you set in the config group, e.g., model type or name to instantiate a model accordingly. 
You can import models from libraries such as HuggingFace transformers or load your own PyTorch checkpoints.

The :code:`num_chunks` argument is a critical one that enables you to balance a higher degree of concurrency 
you desire for cross-config comparisons against the (relatively minor) extra swapping overhead incurred. 
We recommend at least 4, which means you will see results for all runs on 1/4th of the data at a time.



Run Evals
------

The main function to launch LLM evaluation (evals), including with optional RAG, for a given config group in one go. 
See :doc:`the Multi-Config Specification page</configs>` for more details on how to construct a config group.

RapidFire AI can work with three different vector‑store back‑ends:

| Vector‑store backend | Description in the docs |
|----------------------|--------------------------|
| **FAISS** (in‑memory) | The default store used for the built‑in RAG pipeline (GPU‑accelerated exact search). |
| **Pinecone** (hosted) | An external, persistent vector‑DB service that can be called from RapidFire AI. |
| **PGVector** (PostgreSQL) | A self‑hosted or managed PostgreSQL extension for persistent vector storage. |

For the two external stores (Pinecone and PGVector), RapidFire AI defines **three modes of operation** that can be used with each store:

1. **Create mode** – Build a brand‑new index from the base documents supplied inside RapidFire AI and then use that index for RAG.  
2. **Read mode** – Retrieve results from a pre‑existing index (created earlier) and use it for RAG.  
3. **Update mode** – Add new content to an already‑existing index from additional base documents and then use the updated index for RAG.

The documentation states: “Each external store supports three modes of operation: **Create mode**, **Read mode**, **Update mode**” (see the “External Vector Stores: Pinecone and PGVector” section). Thus, RapidFire AI supports FAISS, Pinecone, and PGVector, and the external stores offer the three operations listed above.

Overview of RapidFire AI Package
==============

RapidFire AI is a new AI experiment execution framework that transforms your LLM pipeline customization 
from slow, sequential processes into rapid, intelligent workflows with hyperparallelized execution, 
dynamic real-time experiment control, and automatic backend optimization.

For *RAG and context engineering evals*, start here: :doc:`Install and Get Started: RAG and Context Engineering</walkthroughrag>`.

For *SFT and RFT/post-training workflows*, start here: :doc:`Install and Get Started: SFT/RFT</walkthroughft>`.


RapidFire AI is the first system of its kind to establish live three-way communication between the IDE
where the experiment is launched, a metrics display/control dashboard, and a multi-core/multi-GPU execution backend.

.. image:: /images/rf-usage.png
   :width: 800px
The RAG pipeline uses:

- **Embeddings**: sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 with GPU acceleration.
- **Vector Store**: FAISS with GPU-based exact search, i.e., no ANN approximation.
- **Retrieval**: Top-15 similarity search.
- **Reranking**: cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2 with 2 different top-n values: 2 and 5.

All other knobs are fixed across all configs. Thus, there are a total of 8 combinations launched 
with a simple grid search: 2 generator models x 2 chunk sizes x 2 reranking top-n values.


External Vector Stores: Pinecone and PGVector
-------

RapidFire AI also supports external persistent vector stores beyond the default in-memory FAISS.
This allows you to scale to larger corpora, persist indexes across runs and experiments, and leverage managed vector DBMS services.
As of this writing, **Pinecone** (hosted serverless or pod-based) and **PostgreSQL PGVector** (self-hosted or managed) are supported.

Each external store supports three modes of operation:
Each external store supports three modes of operation:

- **Create mode:** Build a new index from base documents from within RapidFire AI itself and use it for RAG.
- **Read mode:** Retrieve from a pre-existing index and use it for RAG. 
- **Update mode:** Add new content to an existing index from additional base documents from within RapidFire AI itself and use it for RAG. 

See the :doc:`API: LangChain RAG Spec page</ragspecs>` for more details on how to specify these external vector stores.

The FiQA RAG tutorial notebooks have also been extended to showcase the external stores as below:

- **Pinecone**: `View on GitHub <https://github.com/RapidFireAI/rapidfireai/blob/main/tutorial_notebooks/rag-contexteng/rf-tutorial-rag-fiqa-pinecone.ipynb>`__
- **PGVector**: `View on GitHub <https://github.com/RapidFireAI/rapidfireai/blob/main/tutorial_notebooks/rag-contexteng/rf-tutorial-rag-fiqa-pgvector.ipynb>`__
RapidFire AI supports multi-GPU setups natively. Here is a (simplified) illustration of 
sequential execution with Data Parallelism (say, with DDP or FSDP) vs. Task Parallelism 
(say, with Weights & Biases) vs. RapidFire AI, both without and with IC Ops. 
Our scheduler navigates multiple GPUs automatically so that you need not worry if any GPU 
is underutilized, e.g., like in the case of Task Parallelism for the workload shown below.

.. image:: /images/gantt-2gpu.png
   :width: 800px

Likewise, for RAG/context engineering evals on self-hosted LLMs, the above multi-GPU 
scheduling optimizations also apply out of the box, albeit analogous to a single epoch. 
When using only closed model APIs such as OpenAI, RapidFire AI's scheduler automatically 
optimizes how CPU cores and the token rate limits are apportioned across configs. 
This will help avoid wastage of token spend on unproductive RAG configs and help you 
redirect the spend to more productive RAG configs in real time.
.. image:: /images/gantt-1gpu.png
   :width: 800px

In the above figure, all 3 model configs are shown for 1 epoch. RapidFire AI is set to use 4 chunks.
So, before model config 3 (M3) even starts in the sequential approach, RapidFire AI already shows you 
the learning behaviors of all 3 configs on the first 2-3 chunks. 
The overhead of swapping, represented by the thin gray box, is minimal, less than 5% of the runtime,
as per our measurements--thanks to our new efficient memory management techniques.

For inference evals for RAG/context engineering, such sharded execution means RapidFire AI surfaces eval metrics 
sooner based on a statistical technique known as *online aggregation* from the database systems literature.
Basically, see estimated values and confidence intervals for all eval metrics in real time as the shards 
get processed, ultimately converging to the exact metrics on the full dataset.


The Power of Dynamic Real-Time Control
------------
* Even for a prior deployed model, one may need to adapt knobs over time as the data distribution evolves (e.g., concept drift), application schema evolves (e.g., data collection process changes), newer/better models emerge (e.g., smaller but more capable LLMs), etc.


Generic MLOps tools treat a run as a generic monolithic job and schedule them at a coarse granularity, 
leading to a disconnect between what is needed for customization and the execution layer.
IC Ops alter this status quo by giving you a whole new level of control over runs in flight. 

No need to juggle disparate tools for data-parallelism (DDP), model-parallelism (FSDP / DeepSpeed), or 
task-parallelism (W&B, Ray Tune, etc.).
RapidFire AI's execution engine handles lower level scheduling and orchestration of run adaptively 
to enable IC Ops.



Semantics of IC Ops
-----
Run the following commands to initialize rapidfireai to use the correct dependencies for RAG evals:

.. code-block:: bash

   rapidfireai init --evals
   # It will install specific dependencies and initialize rapidfireai for RAG evals


.. note::
  You need to run init **only once** for a new venv or when switching GPU(s) on your machine. You do NOT need to run it after a reboot or for a new terminal tab.


Next start RapidFire AI services: the frontend with the ML metrics dashboard and the API server. 
The frontend URL shown below can be opened on your local browser.

.. code-block:: bash

   rapidfireai start
   # It should print about 50 lines, including the following:
   # ...
   # RapidFire Frontend is ready
   # Open your browser and navigate to: http://0.0.0.0:8853
   # ...
   # Press Ctrl+C to stop all services

.. important::
The Power of Dynamic Real-Time Control
------------

Our adaptive execution engine also enables a powerful new capability: *dynamic real-time 
control over runs in flight*. We call this Interactive Control Operations, or IC Ops for short. 

*Stop* non-promising runs at any point--they will be put on a wait queue. *Resume* any later if 
you want to revisit it. *Clone* high-performing runs from the dashboard and *Modify* the 
configuration knobs as you see fit to try new variations. *Warm start* the clone's parameters 
with the parent's to give them a headstart in learning behavior. 
Under the hood, RapidFire AI automatically manages how runs and chunks are placed on GPUs, 
freeing you to focus fully on the logic of your AI experiment rather than wrestling with 
low-level systems issue to parallelize your work.
.. code-block:: bash

   rapidfireai stop

.. important::
  If you kill the rapidfireai server forcibly without graceful stopping as above, you might lose some experiment artifacts and/or metadata.

.. note::
  Of course, if you did not even start the server in Step 2 since it is optional, there is no need to run the stop command here.



Step 8: Venture Beyond!
-----

After trying out the tutorial notebooks, explore the rest of this docs website, 
especially the API pages for RAG and context engineering. 
Play around more with IC Ops and/or run more experiments as you wish, including 
changing the prompt schemes, generator models and its knobs, chunking / reranking / retrieval knobs, 
and eval metrics definitions.

You are now up to speed! Enjoy the power of rapid AI customization with RapidFire AI!
.. code-block:: python

    # Based on the FiQA PGVector tutorial notebook
    connection = "postgresql+psycopg://rapidfireai:rapidfireai@localhost:6024/rapidfireai"

    # Create mode:
    vector_store_cfg_create={
        "type": "pgvector",
        "connection": connection,
        "batch_size": 1024, # Different from generation batch size. Defaults to 128 if not set
    }

The **`search_cfg`** dictionary must contain a key **`"type"`** whose value can be one of three supported search‑algorithm options:

1. **`"similarity"`** – standard cosine‑similarity search.  
2. **`"similarity_score_threshold"`** – similarity search that applies a minimum score threshold (SST).  
3. **`"mmr"`** – Maximum Marginal Relevance search for diversity.

These three options are listed explicitly in the specification text for the `search_cfg` parameter.

**Notes:**

Note that one :class:`RFLangChainRagSpec` object can have at most one :code:`document_loader` to specify the base data.
But you can specify a :class:`List` or :class:`Range` (when applicable) for all the other knobs in a multi-config specification. 
For instance, the example above showcases two text splitters and two rerankers with different hyperparameters.

Overall, to recap the control flow of the components are as follows:

* If :code:`retriever` is provided, it is used as is. No need for :code:`document_loader`, :code:`text_splitter`, or :code:`vector_store_cfg`.
:param retriever: The retriever for chunk retrieval. If not provided, a default FAISS vector store will be created automatically using the specified search configuration below. Must be a LangChain BaseRetriever implementation.
    :type retriever: BaseRetriever, optional

    :param search_cfg: The search algorithm type and its kwargs to use for retrieval of vectors/chunks, provided as a single dictionary. Must include a key :code:`"type"` with one of the following three options listed as value; default is :code:`"similarity"`.

      * :code:`"similarity"`: Standard cosine similarity search.
      * :code:`"similarity_score_threshold"`: Similarity search with minimum score threshold (SST).
      * :code:`"mmr"`: Maximum Marginal Relevance (MMR) search for diversity.

      Additional parameters for search configuration depend on the type; the keys can include the following:
.. note::
  When constructing a config group with :func:`List()` or :func:`Range()`, the interaction of :code:`k` in :code:`search_cfg` with :code:`top_n` in :code:`reranker_cfg` has a nuance. If the assigned :code:`k` is less than the assigned :code:`top_n`, the combination is meaningless and will be omitted automatically by RapidFire AI. All other combinations will create valid runs. For example, if :code:`k` is :func:`List([5, 10])` and :code:`top_n` is :func:`List([5, 6])`, then in the 2 x 2 grid obtained, the combination :code:`k` = 5 and :code:`top_n` = 6 will be automatically omitted but the other 3 will be valid.

**Online aggregation in RapidFire AI evals**

RapidFire AI treats the evaluation of a RAG / context‑engineering pipeline as a stream of *shards* (randomly‑sampled blocks of the full evaluation set).  
Instead of waiting until the entire dataset has been processed, the system continuously updates **estimated metric values** together with **statistical confidence intervals** after each shard finishes.  
These “online‑aggregated” numbers are shown to the user in real time, and they **converge to the exact point‑estimate** (and a zero‑width interval) once 100 % of the data have been seen.  
This lets you stop poor configurations early, clone promising ones, and generally steer experiments while the run is still in progress.

**Three confidence‑interval strategies**

The documentation states that RapidFire AI “supports **3 strategies** to calculate confidence intervals for projected estimates of metrics.”  
These strategies are configurable under the key `online_strategy_kwargs` in a config dictionary, together with a selectable confidence level (e.g., 95 %) and an optional *finite‑population correction* (FPC).  

> “Based on that, it supports 3 strategies to calculate confidence intervals for projected estimates of metrics. You can indicate the confidence level (we recommend 95 %) and whether to perform ‘finite population correction’ (FPC) or not. These values can be specified under the key `online_strategy_kwargs` in your config dictionary as illustrated below.”

Online Aggregation for Evals
============================

When evaluating RAG/context eng. pipelines, traditional batch evals processing forces you to 
wait for the whole dataset to be processed by a config before seeing its results. 
For expensive LLM-based generators (both closed model APIs and self-hosted models) that can lead
to wastage of a lot of token spend and/or a lot of GPU resources before you realize that a config 
yields poor eval metrics. 
That can inhibit experimentation on config knobs due to the time and/or costs involved, 
ultimately hurting eval metrics and stalling AI applications.

RapidFire AI transforms the status quo by adapting the powerful idea of **online aggregation** 
from database systems research to LLM evals. 
Our adaptive execution engine, :doc:`as described on this page</difference>`, automatically 
shards the data and processes multiple configs in parallel, one shard at a time, with 
efficient swapping techniques.
.. image:: /images/gantt-1gpu.png
   :width: 800px

In the above figure, all 3 model configs are shown for 1 epoch. RapidFire AI is set to use 4 chunks.
So, before model config 3 (M3) even starts in the sequential approach, RapidFire AI already shows you 
the learning behaviors of all 3 configs on the first 2-3 chunks. 
The overhead of swapping, represented by the thin gray box, is minimal, less than 5% of the runtime,
as per our measurements--thanks to our new efficient memory management techniques.

For inference evals for RAG/context engineering, such sharded execution means RapidFire AI surfaces eval metrics 
sooner based on a statistical technique known as *online aggregation* from the database systems literature.
Basically, see estimated values and confidence intervals for all eval metrics in real time as the shards 
get processed, ultimately converging to the exact metrics on the full dataset.


The Power of Dynamic Real-Time Control
------------
This means you get **running metric estimates with confidence intervals** in real time. 
So, you can confidently stop poor configs earlier, clone better configs on the fly, and 
perform more informed exploration to reach much better eval metrics in much less time.

-------

For instance, suppose you have an evals set with 400 queries. You decide to compare, say, 
4 RAG configs in one go with RapidFire AI with number of shards set to 8. The illustration
below contrasts traditional batch evals vs. RapidFire AI's approach for a simple eval metric.

All configs are executed on the first 1/8th of the data (50 examples), with 
their **incrementally computed** eval metrics shown in real time with confidence intervals. 
In the figure, the 3 worst configs are stopped, while the best is cloned to add 2 new variants. 
The 3 running configs now continue on the second 1/8th of the data (cumulatively, 
100 examples), and so on.
One clone is then stopped halfway through the aggregation, while the other two run to completion. 
Ultimately, the other clone ends up being the best config overall.
Takeaways
----------

RapidFire AI transforms RAG/context engineering evals from a slow, tedious 
guessing game into a fast, dynamic engineering process. 
With real-time metrics, statistically sound confidence intervals, and dynamic control, 
you can compare far more configs efficiently, make data-driven decisions, and 
optimize across the Pareto frontier of eval metrics, cost, and time.
Note that the confidence intervals shown will keep narrowing as configs see more shards, converging 
to zero when 100% of the data is seen, i.e., the metrics become exact point estimates.
Overall, compared to sequential batch evals in which the original 4 configs all run to completion, 
RapidFire AI enables you to explore more configs in less time, while reaching better eval metrics.



Types of Metrics
-----------------------

We support 2 types of metrics based on their aggregation semantics: 

* **Distributive Metrics:** These are purely additive over a given set of data points. 
  
  Examples: *count* of number of correct predictions; *sum* of output token lengths across queries.
Why Not Just Downsample?
------------------------

One might wonder why downsampling the eval set does not suffice here. 
:doc:`As also explained on this page</difference>`, downsampling alone has 
significant disadvantages compared to the approach offered by RapidFire AI. 

First, you have to decide a downsample size upfront, which is not trivial if your
eval metrics have high variance across examples. Point estimates without confidence 
intervals can give false confidence in a sample. You can resample manually 
over and over, but that adds manual grunt work of juggling separate samples/files. 
Finally, downsampling alone does not offer you the power of IC Ops and automated 
parallelization to try new configs on the fly--you'd have reimplement those manually.

RapidFire AI's online aggregation approach with IC Ops avoids all the above issues,
while also being **complementary** to downsampling, i.e., you can use both in 
conjunction for even lower runtimes/costs.
Why Not Just Downsample Data?
------------

At first glance, one might consider running multi-config comparisons by downsampling data for 
quick estimates, then running promising configs on full data. While common, this approach is 
often misleading and cumbersome.

A single downsample introduces variance from one static snapshot, potentially leading to wrong 
conclusions, especially with overfitting-prone LLMs/DL models. It requires manual checkpoint 
management, adding tedious file work. You also do not get dynamic control (stop, resume, clone-modify),
or you must reimplement such tricky operations, taking time away from your AI application work.

RapidFire AI takes such practical heuristics to their logical conclusion with shard-based 
adaptive multi-config execution with dynamic experiment control. This offers you maximum power 
and flexibility for AI development without extra DevOps grunt work, i.e., *rapid experimentation*.
Overview of RapidFire AI Package
==============

RapidFire AI is a new AI experiment execution framework that transforms your LLM pipeline customization 
from slow, sequential processes into rapid, intelligent workflows with hyperparallelized execution, 
dynamic real-time experiment control, and automatic backend optimization.

For *RAG and context engineering evals*, start here: :doc:`Install and Get Started: RAG and Context Engineering</walkthroughrag>`.

For *SFT and RFT/post-training workflows*, start here: :doc:`Install and Get Started: SFT/RFT</walkthroughft>`.


RapidFire AI is the first system of its kind to establish live three-way communication between the IDE
where the experiment is launched, a metrics display/control dashboard, and a multi-core/multi-GPU execution backend.

**How to warm‑start a clone with the Clone‑Modify IC Op**

1. Open the **Clone‑Modify** panel for the run you want to copy (the *parent* run).  
2. In the editable text box you will see the parent’s full knob‑config dictionary.  
3. Beside the config editor there is a **Warm‑start** toggle/checkbox.  
4. Turn the toggle on – this tells RapidFire AI to initialise the new clone with the **parent’s checkpoint weights** instead of starting from scratch.  
5. Edit any knobs you wish (learning‑rate, LoRA rank, base model, etc.) and then click **“Submit”**.  
6. The clone will be queued, and at the next chunk boundary RapidFire will spin it up, loading the parent’s weights and applying the new config.

**Constraints that must be satisfied**

- **Identical architecture** – The clone must use exactly the same neural network architecture as the parent, **including any LoRA adapters**. If you change the base model, model size, or add/remove adapters, the system will raise an error and the warm‑start will be rejected.  
- **Same checkpoint format** – Because the clone is seeded from the parent’s saved parameters, the checkpoint files must be compatible; this is automatically enforced by the “identical architecture” rule.  

When these conditions are met, the warm‑started clone inherits the parent’s learning progress, so it can reach better evaluation metrics faster than a fresh run. If the architectures differ, you must start the clone from scratch (no warm‑start).

**Purpose of `accumulate_metrics_fn`**

`accumulate_metrics_fn` is an **optional, user‑provided callback** that is run **once, after all batches have been processed**. Its job is to **aggregate the per‑batch metric dictionaries produced by `compute_metrics_fn` into final, dataset‑wide values**.  
You need it when your metrics are *algebraic*—e.g., averages, precisions, recall, mean ROUGE, or any metric that requires a (weighted) division or other custom combination of the per‑batch components. By supplying this function you can implement the proper logic (such as summing numerators and denominators separately and then dividing) to obtain the correct overall metric and its confidence interval.

**What happens if it is not provided?**

If you do **not** supply an `accumulate_metrics_fn`, the eval system falls back to a default assumption: **all metrics returned by `compute_metrics_fn` are treated as *distributive***. In other words, the framework will simply **sum the per‑batch values** across the whole dataset. This works for purely additive metrics (e.g., counts or sums) but will give incorrect results for algebraic metrics that need averaging or other non‑additive aggregation.

*Key excerpts from the context*:

- “Optional user‑provided function to aggregate algebraic eval metrics across all batches of the data. If this function is not provided, all metrics returned by `eval.compute_metrics_fn()` will be assumed to be distributive (i.e., summed across batches) by default.”  
- “It is invoked once at the very end of the evaluation process after all batches have been processed.”  
- “User‑given evaluation function to aggregate algebraic eval metrics across batches. If this is not given, all metrics provided in `eval_compute_metrics_fn` will be assumed to be distributive by default.”

Thus, `accumulate_metrics_fn` enables correct handling of algebraic metrics; without it, the system defaults to simple summation, suitable only for distributive metrics.

Eval Accumulate Metrics Function
----------------------------

Optional user-provided function to aggregate algebraic eval metrics across all batches of the data. 
If this function is not provided, all metrics returned by :func:`eval.compute_metrics_fn()` 
will be assumed to be distributive (i.e., summed across batches) by default. Use this function 
when metrics require (weighted) averaging or other custom dataset-wide aggregation logic.

It is invoked once at the very end of the evaluation process after all batches have been processed.
Pass it directly to the :code:`accumulate_metrics_fn` key in your eval config dictionary.

Online Aggregation for Evals
============================

When evaluating RAG/context eng. pipelines, traditional batch evals processing forces you to 
wait for the whole dataset to be processed by a config before seeing its results. 
For expensive LLM-based generators (both closed model APIs and self-hosted models) that can lead
to wastage of a lot of token spend and/or a lot of GPU resources before you realize that a config 
yields poor eval metrics. 
That can inhibit experimentation on config knobs due to the time and/or costs involved, 
ultimately hurting eval metrics and stalling AI applications.

RapidFire AI transforms the status quo by adapting the powerful idea of **online aggregation** 
from database systems research to LLM evals. 
Our adaptive execution engine, :doc:`as described on this page</difference>`, automatically 
shards the data and processes multiple configs in parallel, one shard at a time, with 
efficient swapping techniques.

RapidFire AI enables you to explore more configs in less time, while reaching better eval metrics.

-----------------------

We support 2 types of metrics based on their aggregation semantics: 

* **Distributive Metrics:** These are purely additive over a given set of data points. 
  
  Examples: *count* of number of correct predictions; *sum* of output token lengths across queries.

-----
All files related to an experiment saved under in a local folder with its path specified by

Config Dictionary
-----

A dictionary of key-value pairs that specify a full model training configuration. 
A knob's value can be a singleton or set-valued (:class:`List` or :class:`Range`).

RapidFire AI automatically **prunes any grid‑search combination in which the retrieval size `k` is smaller than the reranker’s `top_n`**.  

- When you define a config group with `List()` or `Range()` for the search parameter `k` (inside `search_cfg`) and for the reranker parameter `top_n` (inside `reranker_cfg`), RapidFire AI first builds the full Cartesian product of the two lists.  
- It then checks each pair: **if `k < top_n`, the pair is considered “meaningless” and is dropped**. All other pairs (where `k ≥ top_n`) are kept and will be launched as valid runs.  

The documentation gives a concrete example:  

> “If `k` is `List([5, 10])` and `top_n` is `List([5, 6])`, the 2 × 2 grid would contain the pair `k = 5` / `top_n = 6`. RapidFire AI automatically omits that combination, while the other three combinations (`5‑5`, `10‑5`, `10‑6`) are valid.”  

Thus, the interaction is handled by **auto‑omission of any configuration where the search‑k value is less than the reranker‑top_n value**, ensuring that only sensible config pairs are executed.

The RAG pipeline uses:

Online Aggregation for Evals
============================

When evaluating RAG/context eng. pipelines, traditional batch evals processing forces you to 
wait for the whole dataset to be processed by a config before seeing its results. 
For expensive LLM-based generators (both closed model APIs and self-hosted models) that can lead
to wastage of a lot of token spend and/or a lot of GPU resources before you realize that a config 
yields poor eval metrics. 
That can inhibit experimentation on config knobs due to the time and/or costs involved, 
ultimately hurting eval metrics and stalling AI applications.

RapidFire AI transforms the status quo by adapting the powerful idea of **online aggregation** 
from database systems research to LLM evals. 
Our adaptive execution engine, :doc:`as described on this page</difference>`, automatically 
shards the data and processes multiple configs in parallel, one shard at a time, with 
efficient swapping techniques.
API: Multi-Config Specification
===============

The core value of RapidFire AI is in the ability to launch, compare, and dynamically 
control multiple configurations (configs) in one go. 
It is already common practice in AI to do hyperparameter sweeps via grid search, 
random search, or AutoML heuristics to generate knob values. 

RapidFire AI generalizes that notion to any type of config knobs, not just  
regular hyperparameters, but also base model architectures, prompt schemes, 
LoRA adapters, and optimizers (for training), as well as data chunking, embedding, 
retrieval, reranking, generation, and prompt schemes (for RAG) and any other 
user-defined knobs. 


Knob Set Generators
-------

To create a multi-config specification, you need two things: **knob set generators** for 
knob values and **config group generators** that take a config with set-valued knobs 
to generate groups of full configs.

The kwargs that follow must contain all parameters needed to initialize the reranker class; required parameters vary by reranker class. as per our measurements--thanks to our new efficient memory management techniques.

For inference evals for RAG/context engineering, such sharded execution means RapidFire AI surfaces eval metrics 
sooner based on a statistical technique known as *online aggregation* from the database systems literature.
Basically, see estimated values and confidence intervals for all eval metrics in real time as the shards 
get processed, ultimately converging to the exact metrics on the full dataset.


The Power of Dynamic Real-Time Control
------------
This means you get **running metric estimates with confidence intervals** in real time. 
So, you can confidently stop poor configs earlier, clone better configs on the fly, and 
perform more informed exploration to reach much better eval metrics in much less time.


Example: Traditional Batch Evals vs. RapidFire AI
-------

For instance, suppose you have an evals set with 400 queries. You decide to compare, say, 
4 RAG configs in one go with RapidFire AI with number of shards set to 8. The illustration
below contrasts traditional batch evals vs. RapidFire AI's approach for a simple eval metric.

Note that the return types of the knob set generators are internal to RapidFire AI and 
they are usable only within the context of the config group generators below.



Config Group Generators
-----

We currently support two common config group generators: :func:`RFGridSearch()` for grid search 
and :func:`RFRandomSearch()` for random search. 

More support for AutoML heuristics such as SHA, HyperOpt, as well as an integration with 
the popular AutoML library Optuna are coming soon. 
Likewise for RAG/context engineering, we also plan to support the AutoML heuristic syftr.

	:param configs: A config dictionary with :func:`List()` for at least one knob; can be a list of such config dictionaries too.
	:type configs: Dict[str, Any] | List[Dict[str, Any]]
Why Not Just Downsample Data?
------------

At first glance, one might consider running multi-config comparisons by downsampling data for 
quick estimates, then running promising configs on full data. While common, this approach is 
often misleading and cumbersome.

A single downsample introduces variance from one static snapshot, potentially leading to wrong 
conclusions, especially with overfitting-prone LLMs/DL models. It requires manual checkpoint 
management, adding tedious file work. You also do not get dynamic control (stop, resume, clone-modify),
or you must reimplement such tricky operations, taking time away from your AI application work.

RapidFire AI takes such practical heuristics to their logical conclusion with shard-based 
adaptive multi-config execution with dynamic experiment control. This offers you maximum power 
and flexibility for AI development without extra DevOps grunt work, i.e., *rapid experimentation*.

**How `document_template` works**

- In an **`RFLangChainRagSpec`** you can pass a **`document_template`** argument that is *optional* but, when supplied, controls exactly how each retrieved LangChain **`Document`** is turned into a string that will be inserted into the prompt (the “context injection” step).  
- The value must be a **callable** with the signature `Callable[[Document], str]`.  
- The callable receives a single `Document` instance, giving you access to both its `page_content` (the text) and its `metadata` dictionary.  
- Whatever string the function returns is what RapidFire AI will use for that chunk.  
- When several documents are returned, RapidFire AI simply **joins the formatted strings with a double‑newline (`"\n\n"`)** before feeding them to the generator.

> *“:param document_template: Optional function to format each retrieved chunk for context injection into prompts. Should accept a single LangChain :class:`Document` object and return a formatted string. Multiple documents are separated by double newlines when serialized.”* (context)

**Default template behavior**

If you do **not** provide a custom `document_template`, RapidFire AI falls back to an internal default function:

```python
def default_template(doc: Document) -> str:
    """Default document formatting template."""
    metadata = "; ".join([f"{k}: {v}" for k, v in doc.metadata.items()])
    return f"{metadata}:\n{doc.page_content}"
```

- It first builds a single line that concatenates **all metadata key‑value pairs**, each formatted as `"key: value"` and separated by a semicolon and a space (`"; "`).  
- It then places a colon and a newline, followed by the document’s actual text (`doc.page_content`).  

Thus, by default every chunk appears as:

```
key1: value1; key2: value2; ...:
<document text>
```

**Typical custom usage**

The documentation shows two concrete examples:

1. **Using a title field extracted by `metadata_func`:**

   ```python
   def custom_template(doc: Document) -> str:
       return f"{doc.metadata['title']}: {doc.page_content}"
   ```

2. **Including only a specific metadata field (e.g., `source`):**

   ```python
   def sample_template(doc: Document) -> str:
       doc_source = doc.metadata.get("source", "")
       return f"Document Source: {doc_source}:\nContent: {doc.page_content}"
   ```

These examples illustrate how you can tailor the injected context—choosing which metadata to show and how to format it—by supplying your own `document_template` when constructing the `RFLangChainRagSpec`.

API: LangChain RAG Spec
===============

RapidFire AI's core API for defining the stages of a RAG pipeline before the generator is a wrapper around the corresponding APIs of LangChain.
In particular, this class specifies all of the following stages: data loading, chunking, embedding, indexing, retrieval, and reranking steps. 
Note that many of these stages are optional. 

Many of the arguments (knobs) here can also be :class:`List` valued or :class:`Range` valued depending 
on its data type, as explained below. All this forms the base set of knob combinations from which 
a config group can be produced. Also read :doc:`the Multi-Config Specification page</configs>`.
.. image:: /images/rf-usage.png
   :width: 800px

Just pip install the :code:`rapidfireai` OSS package. It works on a CPU-only machine, a single-GPU machine, 
or a multi-GPU machine. Note that for RAG/context engineering with only closed model APIs, GPUs are not needed. 

Launch the server from the command line. Then import it as any other python package in your notebook/script. 
Use our API to define and launch the configs to compare in one go. 

Metrics plots are automatically visualized in the ML metrics dashboard (for SFT/RFT only for now) or shown in an 
in-notebook take (for RAG/context eng. only for now). 
The Interactive Control (IC) ops panel lets you dynamically control runs in flight: stop, resume, clone, and modify them as you wish.

Check out :doc:`the step-by-step walkthrough page</walkthrough>` and watch the usage video for details.

**What `run_evals()` returns**

- The documentation states that **`run_evals()` does have a return value**.  
- Specifically, it “will return a **dictionary** with the **run/config ID as the key**.  
- The associated value is a **2‑tuple**:  

  1. **A dictionary of all aggregated metrics** for that run/config.  
  2. **A dictionary of all cumulative metrics** for that run/config.  

> “Unlike :func:`run_fit()`, this function does have a return value. In particular, it will return a dictionary with the run/config ID as the key. The value is a 2‑tuple with a dictionary each for all aggregated metrics and all cumulative metrics.” (Context)

**How this differs from `run_fit()`**

- `run_fit()` **does not return anything** (its return type is `None`). It is used to launch training jobs and only affects internal experiment state.  
- `run_evals()`, on the other hand, **produces a concrete result object** (the dictionary described above) that you can inspect programmatically immediately after the evaluation finishes.

So, while `run_fit()` is fire‑and‑forget (no return), `run_evals()` gives you a structured summary of each evaluation run’s metrics, enabling downstream post‑processing or decision‑making.

API: Generator Configs
===============

RapidFire AI supports both self-hosted open LLMs and closed model LLM APIs as the generator. 
As of this writing, it wraps around the model config of vLLM for the former and the OpenAI API for the latter. 
We plan to expand support for more generator plugins, including Gemini and Claude APIs, based on feedback. 


RFvLLMModelConfig
------

This is a wrapper around vLLM's :class:`config` and :class:`SamplingParams` classes. 
The full list of their arguments are available on `this page <https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/api/vllm/config/index.html>`__ 
and `this page <https://docs.vllm.ai/en/v0.6.4/dev/sampling_params.html>`__, respectively.
API: Multi-Config Specification
===============

The core value of RapidFire AI is in the ability to launch, compare, and dynamically 
control multiple configurations (configs) in one go. 
It is already common practice in AI to do hyperparameter sweeps via grid search, 
random search, or AutoML heuristics to generate knob values. 

RapidFire AI generalizes that notion to any type of config knobs, not just  
regular hyperparameters, but also base model architectures, prompt schemes, 
LoRA adapters, and optimizers (for training), as well as data chunking, embedding, 
retrieval, reranking, generation, and prompt schemes (for RAG) and any other 
user-defined knobs. 


Knob Set Generators
-------

To create a multi-config specification, you need two things: **knob set generators** for 
knob values and **config group generators** that take a config with set-valued knobs 
to generate groups of full configs.
Suppose you have only 1 GPU, say an A100 or H100, and you want to run SFT on a Llama model. 
Current tools force you to run one config after another *sequentially* as shown in the (simplified) illustration below. 
In contrast, by operating on shards, RapidFire AI offers a far more concurrent learning experience by 
automatically *swapping* adapters (and base models, if needed) across GPU(s) and DRAM. 
It does this via efficient shared memory-based caching mechanisms that can spill to disk when needed.

.. image:: /images/gantt-1gpu.png
   :width: 800px
Overview of RapidFire AI Package
==============

RapidFire AI is a new AI experiment execution framework that transforms your LLM pipeline customization 
from slow, sequential processes into rapid, intelligent workflows with hyperparallelized execution, 
dynamic real-time experiment control, and automatic backend optimization.

For *RAG and context engineering evals*, start here: :doc:`Install and Get Started: RAG and Context Engineering</walkthroughrag>`.

For *SFT and RFT/post-training workflows*, start here: :doc:`Install and Get Started: SFT/RFT</walkthroughft>`.


RapidFire AI is the first system of its kind to establish live three-way communication between the IDE
where the experiment is launched, a metrics display/control dashboard, and a multi-core/multi-GPU execution backend.

.. image:: /images/rf-usage.png
   :width: 800px
Note that the return types of the knob set generators are internal to RapidFire AI and 
they are usable only within the context of the config group generators below.



Config Group Generators
-----

We currently support two common config group generators: :func:`RFGridSearch()` for grid search 
and :func:`RFRandomSearch()` for random search. 

More support for AutoML heuristics such as SHA, HyperOpt, as well as an integration with 
the popular AutoML library Optuna are coming soon. 
Likewise for RAG/context engineering, we also plan to support the AutoML heuristic syftr.

Multi-GPU Model Partitioning with FSDP
-------

RapidFire AI supports automated large model partitioning across GPUs (on the same machine) via PyTorch's native FSDP. 
Provide the relevant FSDP deatils in a config knob, optionally along with the number of GPUs to use for that run. 
The following notebooks showcase the use of FSDP for SFT with the corresponding LLMs:

* FSDP Lite with base model TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0. Needs at least 2x A10 GPUs or equivalent (48 GB total HBM) to work. `View on GitHub <https://github.com/RapidFireAI/rapidfireai/blob/main/tutorial_notebooks/fine-tuning/rf-tutorial-sft-chatqa-fsdp-lite.ipynb>`__
What Makes RapidFire AI Different?
==============

The crux of RapidFire AI's difference is in its *adaptive execution engine*: it enables "interruptible"
execution of configurations across GPUs/CPUs. To do so, it first shards the training and/or evaluation 
dataset randomly into "chunks" (also called "shards").
Then instead of waiting for a run to see the whole dataset for all epochs (for SFT/RFT) or for full 
eval metrics calculation (for RAG evals), RapidFire AI schedules all runs on *one shard at a time*, 
and then cycles through all shards.

**Rate‑limiting knobs in `RFOpenAIAPIModelConfig`**

`RFOpenIOAPIModelConfig` exposes two explicit throttling parameters:

| Parameter | Type | What it controls | Why it’s needed |
|-----------|------|------------------|----------------|
| **`rpm_limit`** | `int` | Maximum number of **requests per minute** sent to the OpenAI API. | Prevents the client from issuing more calls than the per‑minute quota allowed for your OpenAI tier, avoiding “429 Too Many Requests” errors. |
| **`tpm_limit`** | `int` | Maximum number of **tokens per minute** consumed by the API (including both prompt and completion tokens). | Ensures the total token flow stays within the token‑per‑minute limits published by OpenAI, protecting you from exceeding your quota and incurring rate‑limit blocks. |

The documentation explicitly states that these limits are “used for throttling to avoid exceeding API quotas” and that you should “check the rate limit published by Open AI for details on your tier and the latest per‑model limits” (see the description of `rpm_limit` and `tpm_limit` in the context). Without these knobs, RapidFire AI could unintentionally flood the OpenAI endpoint, leading to failed calls and potential service interruptions.
